text: Making cold brew at home starts with a coarse grind—aim for something close to raw sugar in texture, since a fine grind will slip through your filter and turn the batch murky. Combine the grounds with cold, filtered water at roughly a 1-to-4 ratio for a concentrate, stirring gently to make sure every ground is saturated. Cover the container and let it steep at room temperature or in the fridge for 12 to 18 hours, tasting toward the end to find the strength you like. When it's ready, strain the coffee through a fine-mesh sieve lined with cheesecloth or a paper filter, then repeat once more to catch the fine sediment. Dilute the concentrate with water or milk to taste, pour over ice, and store the rest in the fridge for up to two weeks.

text: Starting a compost pile at home is one of the simplest ways to turn kitchen scraps and yard waste into something genuinely useful, and it takes far less effort than most people assume. Before you toss a single banana peel, decide where the composting will happen: a shaded corner of the yard, a lidded bin on a balcony, or a countertop caddy that feeds a larger system. If you have outdoor space, a simple enclosure made from wire mesh or a repurposed plastic bin with drainage holes works fine, and you don't need to buy anything fancy to get started. Apartment dwellers can compost too, either with a sealed worm bin tucked under the sink or by collecting scraps in the freezer and dropping them at a community garden or municipal program. The goal at this stage is just to lower the barrier so that composting becomes a habit rather than a chore you keep putting off. The heart of good compost is balance between two kinds of material, and once you understand it the rest becomes intuitive. "Greens" are the wet, nitrogen-rich items—fruit and vegetable scraps, coffee grounds, fresh grass clippings, and eggshells—while "browns" are the dry, carbon-rich materials like shredded cardboard, dead leaves, paper towels, and small twigs. A healthy pile leans toward more browns than greens, roughly two or three parts brown to one part green by volume, because too many greens turn the pile into a wet, smelly mess. Chop or tear larger pieces into smaller bits so they break down faster, and keep a bag of dry leaves or shredded paper nearby to toss on top whenever you add food scraps. Just as important is knowing what to leave out: meat, dairy, oily foods, and pet waste attract pests and create odors, so keep those out of a home system entirely. With your materials sorted, the day-to-day routine is mostly about maintaining moisture and air. Your pile should feel like a wrung-out sponge—damp but not dripping—so add water during dry spells and extra browns if it ever gets soggy. Oxygen is what keeps the helpful microbes working and the smell at bay, so turn or fluff the pile with a pitchfork or aerator every week or two to mix fresh material into the center. A well-tended pile will actually heat up in the middle, which is a good sign that decomposition is happening efficiently. If it starts to smell sour, it usually means too much moisture or not enough air, and the fix is simply to add browns and give it a thorough turn. Don't panic over small problems; composting is forgiving, and almost any imbalance can be corrected with a handful of leaves or a good stir. Patience is the final ingredient, because finished compost takes anywhere from two months to a year depending on your climate, materials, and how often you turn the pile. You'll know it's ready when the material is dark and crumbly, smells like rich earth rather than garbage, and you can no longer recognize the scraps you put in. At that point, sift out any large chunks that haven't fully broken down and toss them back into the active pile to keep working. Spread the finished compost around garden beds, mix it into potting soil, or top-dress your lawn to feed the plants and improve the soil's ability to hold water. Over time you'll get a feel for the rhythm of your particular setup, adjusting the greens-to-browns ratio and turning schedule to suit the seasons. More than anything, remember that every bin of compost is waste you kept out of a landfill, and that small, steady habit adds up to a real difference.

text: Mara inherited the clock shop the way you inherit a stubborn old dog: not because you asked for it, but because no one else would take it in. Her uncle had run the place for forty years, and when he died the lawyer handed her a brass key and a ledger written in a hand so cramped it looked like a fence line. The shop sat between a bakery and a shuttered pharmacy on a street that had mostly given up on foot traffic. On the first morning she unlocked the door, three hundred clocks were ticking, and not one of them agreed on the time. She meant to sell it. She told herself this while she dusted the walnut cases, while she oiled the escapements, while she learned, almost against her will, the difference between a lever and a cylinder movement. The old regulars kept coming anyway. There was a retired ferry captain who wound his father's marine chronometer every Thursday and never bought a thing. There was a girl of about nine who pressed her nose to the window each afternoon and mouthed the names of the birds carved into the cuckoo cases. Mara found she was staying open later than she needed to, listening to the shop breathe in a thousand small metal heartbeats, and the "for sale" sign she had bought stayed face-down in a drawer. The trouble arrived in October, in the form of a letter from the city. The block was being redeveloped, the letter explained, and the shop's lease would not be renewed past the spring. Mara sat on the stool behind the counter and felt the whole weight of it settle on her, forty years of somebody else's patience about to be swept into a skip. She thought about the captain, and the girl, and the way the light came through the front window at four o'clock and turned the brass to honey. For the first time she understood that she had stopped planning to leave sometime in the summer without ever deciding to stay. So she did the only thing that made sense to her, which was to teach. She put a small hand-lettered card in the window offering free lessons to anyone who wanted to learn to keep a clock running, and to her surprise the room filled. The captain taught knots he swore were relevant. The nine-year-old, whose name turned out to be Posy, had steadier hands than any adult and a memory like a snare. By spring the shop had moved three streets over into a narrower space with a better lease, and half the clocks went with it, carried by the very people who had come to fix them. Mara never did sell the place. She had thought she was inheriting a burden, and it took her almost a year to see that what she'd really been handed was a way to make time belong to more than one person at once.

text: The debate over remote work usually centers on productivity metrics and commute times, but for people in the first few years of their careers the stakes are different and, I would argue, more serious. My position is that fully remote work tends to hurt early-career employees, not because they cannot do the tasks assigned to them, but because it quietly strips away the informal learning that turns a competent beginner into a capable professional. A junior employee's real job is not only to complete tickets or draft reports; it is to absorb judgment, context, and unwritten norms that no onboarding document ever captures. When that absorption depends on being in the room, distance becomes a hidden tax on growth. The convenience of working from home is real, but for someone still figuring out how the work actually gets done, convenience is not the same as advantage. Consider how much of early professional development happens by accident. A new analyst overhears how a senior colleague pushes back on an unreasonable deadline, or watches how a manager reframes a tense client call, and learns something that would have taken months to discover alone. These moments are almost impossible to schedule, and they rarely survive the translation to a video call, where cameras are off, side conversations vanish, and every interaction has to be deliberately initiated. Remote work replaces the ambient, low-stakes exposure of an office with a series of formal meetings that reward people who already know what to ask. Beginners, by definition, do not yet know what they do not know, so the burden of seeking help falls hardest on those least equipped to carry it. The result is that confident, well-connected newcomers still thrive, while quieter or less experienced ones drift, unnoticed, until a performance review makes their isolation official. None of this means remote work is inherently harmful or that offices are magically nurturing; plenty of in-person workplaces ignore their juniors just as thoroughly. Remote arrangements offer genuine benefits, including access to jobs regardless of geography, relief for those with caregiving responsibilities, and freedom from punishing commutes that drain energy better spent on the work itself. A disciplined hybrid model, with intentional mentorship and regular in-person time, can capture much of that flexibility while preserving the human contact beginners need. The problem is that the flexibility tends to be distributed unevenly, and early-career workers are the ones with the least leverage to demand structured support. Left to default, remote culture optimizes for the autonomy of experienced staff who already have networks and reputations to coast on. That default is precisely what fails the people who have neither. So the honest conclusion is not that remote work is good or bad in the abstract, but that its costs land disproportionately on those at the start of their careers. If organizations want to keep the flexibility without sacrificing their next generation of talent, they have to treat mentorship as infrastructure rather than a happy accident. That means deliberate pairing, protected in-person time, and managers who are measured on how well their juniors grow, not just on what ships. Until that effort becomes standard, I believe early-career employees are usually better served by environments that put them close to the people they are trying to become. Flexibility can be earned once the foundation is built; for beginners, the foundation should come first.

text: Starting a backyard vegetable garden is one of the most rewarding projects you can take on, and you don't need much to begin. Pick a spot that gets at least six hours of sunlight a day, and start small—a single raised bed or even a few large containers is plenty for your first season. Trying to plant an entire yard at once is the fastest way to feel overwhelmed, so give yourself room to learn as you go. Focus on vegetables that are forgiving for beginners. Tomatoes, lettuce, zucchini, radishes, and green beans all grow quickly and don't demand much fuss, which means you'll see results and stay motivated. Before you plant, spend a little time improving your soil with compost; healthy soil does more for your harvest than almost anything else you can buy. Watering is where many first-timers stumble. Aim for deep, consistent watering a few times a week rather than a light sprinkle every day, since deeper watering encourages stronger roots. Check your plants every morning if you can—it only takes a few minutes to spot pests, wilting, or ripe produce ready to pick. Most importantly, be patient with yourself. Some plants will thrive and others will flop, and that's simply part of gardening. Every season teaches you something new, so keep notes on what worked, celebrate your first homegrown meal, and enjoy the process of growing food with your own hands.

It is great fun looking through other people's windows, and getting a peep into comedies and tragedies sometimes. text: I worked at big companies for the first 15yrs of my career. And startups for the past 5yrs. Firstly, startups have been an absolute delight. I very carefully chose the company and hence my boss and my co-workers and love working with every engineer on the team. It is a pleasure coming into work each day and I often cant leave because I'm excited about my work. I have a lot of authority over what I build a much of it is "close to the metal" rather than some side system. I get to see the whole slice of cake from conception all the way to sales and client implementations and participate in all of it. At small companies, as an Engineer, I learned how to build a successful product and learned all the steps from inception to sales and production. At every big company I was at, there was more specialization and lots of process. Process was necessary at that size. There was also a great deal of inter-departmental politics and incentives were usually not aligned at big companies, sometimes incentives across departments were even orthogonal. I spent 30% of my time on process and communication at big companies and it went to 80%+ once I was a senior executive. I made a lot of money there, but I think it was to compensate for having to deal with the inner workings of a big company (and being able to be effective at it.) At big companies, I learned how to turn the gears of organizations and learn how to make globe-spanning change effectively. To be fair, I took a big pay-cut to come to a startup as an Engineer. I'm happy with the choice. I dont think there is any silver bullet out there, but it is important to understand what you get with each choice. It is also important to make that choice with full intent and not be fooled or brow-beaten by anyone.
